rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Plants adapt to their water regime with opposite toolkits. Hydrophytes — Hydrilla, lotus, water hyacinth — live with excess: aerenchyma for buoyancy and aeration, reduced roots and xylem, thin cuticles, floating leaves with upper-surface stomata, dissected submerged leaves.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Hydrophyte adaptations: aerenchyma + floating leaves + reduced roots + upper-surface stomata + thin cuticle
Xerophyte adaptations: thick cuticle + spines (modified leaves) + succulent stem + deep roots + CAM photosynthesis
CAM photosynthesis: fix CO2 at night (malic acid) → decarboxylate by day (reduced water loss)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Aerenchyma vs parenchyma:** aerenchyma is parenchyma with large air spaces — buoyancy and aeration; ordinary parenchyma packs tissue.  ·  **Phylloclade vs cladode:** phylloclade = flattened stem doing leaf's job (Opuntia); cladode = one-internode stem-leaf (Asparagus).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a clear hydrophyte vs xerophyte comparison with specific adaptations.  ·  The cactus spines (modified leaves) and succulent stem are key exam points.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Opuntia*** — phylloclade: the cactus "leaf" that is really a water-storing photosynthetic stem.  ·  ***Nymphaea (lotus)*** — floating leaf with upper-surface stomata and aerenchymatous petioles.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Short answer (2m):** What is aerenchyma? **Answer.** A modified **parenchyma tissue with large intercellular air spaces**, characteristic of hydrophytes. It gives buoyancy to floating organs and conducts oxygen down to the roots buried in oxygen-poor anaerobic mud.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Adaptation trade-offs:** every adaptation costs something — spines save water but lose photosynthetic area; aerenchyma saves effort but weakens the stem. Evolution balances, never perfects.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Hydrophytes: aerenchyma, reduced roots/xylem, thin cuticle, stomata upper surface (floating) or absent (submerged), dissected submerged leaves, mucilage — Hydrilla, Nymphaea, Eichhornia.  ·  Xerophytes: deep tap roots, succulent stems (phylloclade), spiny leaves, sunken stomata, thick cuticle, CAM, ephemeral cycles — Opuntia, Aloe, Nerium, Acacia.  ·  Mesophytes: moderate water, no special equipment.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: CAM plants lose 3–6 times less water per unit carbon fixed than ordinary C3 plants.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Xerophyte vs halophyte:** xerophytes face water deficit generally; halophytes face salt stress (mangroves with salt glands).  ·  CAM photosynthesis (xerophytes) is a frequent physiological question.  ·  Differentiate structural, physiological, and behavioural adaptations.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note that adaptation is evolutionary, not individual (acclimatisation is individual).  ·  Pay attention to key terminology in Ecological Adaptation.  ·  Connect this topic to other biological concepts.
